1.title: Plitvice Lakes: Upper & Lower Lakes in a Day

periods.title: Lower Lakes & Great Waterfall
periods.text: Enter through Entrance 1 and take the boat across Kozjak Lake, the largest of Plitvice's 16 interconnected lakes. Descend to the Lower Lakes canyon where the turquoise water is almost unreal, flowing over travertine barriers between pools. Follow the boardwalk trail to Veliki Slap (Great Waterfall), Croatia's tallest at 78 metres, thundering into a mossy pool. The morning light filtering through beech forest canopy makes the water glow emerald and cyan.
periods.tip: Arrive at Entrance 1 by 7am (summer) or 8am (spring/autumn). By 10am the Lower Lakes boardwalks are packed solid.

periods.title: Upper Lakes & Forest Trails
periods.text: Take the panoramic train from the Lower Lakes area up to the Upper Lakes. Walk the wooden boardwalks through Galovac, Gradinsko, and Prošćansko jezero, quieter and greener than the Lower Lakes with waterfalls cascading through dense beech and fir forest. The water changes colour from turquoise to deep blue depending on mineral content and light angle. The whole landscape was formed by calcium-carbonate deposits building natural dams over thousands of years.
periods.tip: The Upper Lakes trail (Route H, 4–6 hours) loops the full park. Bring water and snacks, as there's only one kiosk.

periods.title: Rastoke Village & Dinner
periods.text: Drive 35 minutes north to Rastoke, a tiny village where the Slunjčica River tumbles over waterfalls directly through the houses and mills. It's called "the small lakes" by locals and is far less crowded than Plitvice. Walk the riverside path past water mills, cascades, and swimming holes. Dinner at a Plitvice guesthouse: try ćevapi (grilled minced meat, €7–9), or fresh trout from a local farm served with blitva (Swiss chard and potato).
periods.tip: Rastoke charges a small entrance fee (€2) but is completely empty by late afternoon, so visit after 5pm for a peaceful stroll.

periods.title: Entrance 1 & Lower Lakes Canyon
periods.text: Enter at Entrance 1 (tickets €30 Jul–Aug, €23.50 other months). Descend into the Lower Lakes canyon where a network of wooden boardwalks winds between cascading turquoise pools. The travertine barriers, natural dams built by calcium carbonate deposits, create a staircase of waterfalls connecting pool to pool. Follow the trail to Veliki Slap (Great Waterfall, 78m), Croatia's highest, plunging into a misty pool surrounded by moss-covered cliffs.
periods.tip: Buy tickets online in advance, as summer slots sell out. Arrive before 8am for near-empty boardwalks and the best photography light.

periods.title: Kozjak Lake & Boat Crossing
periods.text: Walk along the lakeside trail to Kozjak, Plitvice's largest lake, 2.3km long and 46m deep. Take the free electric ferry across the jade-green water (included in ticket). The crossing offers panoramic views of the forested hills surrounding the lakes. Disembark at the south shore and explore the quiet trails around Milanovac waterfall and the Supljara Cave, a mossy grotto behind a waterfall curtain.
periods.tip: The ferry queues get long after 11am, so time your crossing for early afternoon when the morning rush has cleared.

periods.title: Plitvice Village & Local Dining
periods.text: Head to one of the guesthouses or restaurants near the park. Lička Kuća restaurant serves traditional Lika cuisine in a rustic wooden interior: lamb cooked under a peka (iron dome), trout from local streams, and štrukli (cheese pastry). A hearty meal runs €15–22. The area around Plitvice village is peaceful in the evening, with forest walks, birdwatching, and complete silence once the day trippers leave.
periods.tip: Book accommodation in Selište Drežničko or Rakovica village, cheaper than lakeside hotels and within 10 minutes of both entrances.

periods.title: Entrance 2 & Upper Lakes
periods.text: Enter through Entrance 2 at the Upper Lakes, where there are far fewer crowds than Entrance 1. Walk Route C along the string of upper lakes: Galovac, Gradinsko, and Okrugljak. Each lake is a different shade of green and blue, connected by curtains of waterfalls and rapids flowing over moss-covered travertine. The Upper Lakes are surrounded by denser forest of beech, fir, and spruce, with wildflowers along the boardwalks in spring and early summer.
periods.tip: Entrance 2 is quieter and has easier parking. Start here for the Upper Lakes and work down, and you'll walk against the crowds.

periods.title: Prošćansko Jezero & Panoramic Train
periods.text: Continue to Prošćansko Jezero, the highest and second-largest lake, fed by the Matica and Crna Rijeka rivers. The trail along its western shore passes through untouched forest with only the sound of flowing water and birdsong. This is the most peaceful section of the park. Take the panoramic train back to Entrance 2 through the forest, free with your park ticket. The train passes viewpoints overlooking the entire lake system.
periods.tip: Prošćansko Jezero is the least visited major lake. If you want solitude in Plitvice, this is where you'll find it.

periods.title: Rastoke Mill Village
periods.text: Drive 35 minutes north to Rastoke at the confluence of the Slunjčica and Korana rivers. This living water-mill village has cascading waterfalls flowing through and around the houses, which earned it the nickname "Little Plitvice." Walk the riverside path past working mills and swimming holes. Dinner at Petro's Restaurant on the riverbank, with grilled trout, potatoes, local wine, and tables overlooking the waterfalls (mains €10–16).
periods.tip: Rastoke is best in late afternoon light when the waterfalls catch golden sun. Visit after 5pm when day-trippers from Zagreb have left.

periods.title: Baraćeve Caves & Lika Countryside
periods.text: Drive 20 minutes to Baraćeve Caves near Nova Kršlja, two limestone caverns with stalactites, stalagmites, and cave formations millions of years old. Guided tours (€8, 45 min) take you through chambers with names like "Concert Hall" and "Petrified Waterfall." The surrounding Lika region is Croatia's wild interior: rolling green hills, scattered villages, and almost no tourists. This is where Zagreb families come for weekend lamb roasts.
periods.tip: Baraćeve Caves stay at 10°C year-round, so bring a jacket even in summer. Tours run hourly from 10am to 4pm.

periods.title: Korana River Swimming & Kayaking
periods.text: Head to the Korana River downstream from Plitvice, the turquoise river that flows out of the lakes. At Korana Village, locals swim in natural pools and off riverside rocks. Rent a kayak (€20 for 2 hours) and paddle through a canyon of green forest with the water so clear you can see every stone on the riverbed. The Korana is warmer than the lakes (swimming in Plitvice lakes is forbidden) and perfect for a hot afternoon.
periods.tip: Korana Village has a small beach area with a bar, perfect for a lazy afternoon. Bring a towel and water shoes for the rocky riverbed.

periods.title: Farewell Dinner & Stargazing
periods.text: Farewell dinner at a local konoba (tavern). Try janjetina ispod peke (lamb slow-cooked under an iron bell with potatoes, €15–18 per person, order in advance). The Lika region has some of Croatia's darkest skies due to minimal light pollution, so step outside after dinner and the Milky Way stretches overhead. Plitvice area accommodation hosts often set up outdoor seating for exactly this purpose.
periods.tip: Order peka lamb at least 3 hours in advance, as it takes that long to cook. Ask your guesthouse to arrange it for dinner.

budgetTips.title: Park tickets
budgetTips.text: Plitvice tickets cost €23.50 (low season) to €30 (Jul–Aug). Buy online to guarantee entry, as summer days sell out. Two-day tickets save money if you want both Upper and Lower Lakes properly.

budgetTips.title: Accommodation hack
budgetTips.text: Skip the overpriced park hotels. Guesthouses in Rakovica, Selište Drežničko, and Jezerce villages are €30–50/double room and within 10 minutes of both entrances. Many include breakfast.

budgetTips.title: Self-cater
budgetTips.text: The park's only restaurant is expensive. Pack sandwiches and water, as picnicking on benches along the trails is allowed. Stock up at Konzum supermarket in Korenica (15 min drive) for €5–8 per day.

budgetTips.title: Transport
budgetTips.text: A rental car is almost essential, as buses from Zagreb (2.5 hours, €12–15) are limited. Split a car rental (€25–35/day) with other travellers. Fuel is about €1.50/litre. Parking at Entrance 1 or 2 is €1.50/hour.

budgetTips.title: Free alternatives
budgetTips.text: Rastoke village (€2 entry), Korana River swimming (free), Slunj fortress ruins (free), and evening stargazing cost almost nothing and rival the park for beauty.

budgetTips.title: Shoulder season
budgetTips.text: May and September offer lower ticket prices, fewer crowds, and beautiful weather. The lakes are more dramatic in spring with higher water levels and stronger waterfalls.

budgetBreakdown.notes: Hostel bed → guesthouse double → park hotel
Bus → shared rental car → private hire
Supermarket beer → konoba wine → cocktail bars

practicalInfo.title: Visa & Entry
items: Croatia joined Schengen Jan 2023, so 90 days visa-free for EU/US/UK/AU/CA/NZ within any 180-day period
Nearest airports: Zagreb (ZAG, 2 hours) or Zadar (ZAD, 1.5 hours). No direct public transport to Plitvice from airports
Buses from Zagreb (2.5 hours, €12–15) and Split (4.5 hours, €18–25) stop at park entrances. Limited schedules, so check Flixbus

practicalInfo.title: Health & Safety
items: No special vaccinations required. EHIC covers EU citizens. Travel insurance essential for non-EU visitors
Tap water is safe throughout Croatia. Bring reusable bottles, as the park has limited water refill points
Stick to marked trails, as the terrain around the lakes has sinkholes and slippery travertine. Bears live in the forest but avoid humans

practicalInfo.title: Getting Around
items: A rental car is strongly recommended, as public transport is limited to 2–3 buses per day from Zagreb/Split
Park transport (electric boats and panoramic trains) is included in your ticket. Trains run every 20–30 minutes
Roads around Plitvice are good but narrow and winding. Watch for wildlife crossings at dawn and dusk

practicalInfo.title: Connectivity
items: Mobile signal is patchy inside the park, so download offline maps before arriving. Strong signal in villages
EU roaming included for European SIM cards. Croatian prepaid SIMs from A1, T-Mobile (€10–15 for 5GB)
WiFi available at most guesthouses. The park itself has WiFi only at entrance areas and the main restaurant

practicalInfo.title: Money
items: Euro (€). Croatia switched from kuna to euro in January 2023. Cards widely accepted at park and hotels
Carry cash for small village restaurants, guesthouses, and market stalls, as many are cash-only
Tipping: Not expected but appreciated. Rounding up to the nearest euro or leaving 10% at restaurants is generous

practicalInfo.title: Packing Tips
items: Waterproof hiking shoes are essential, as boardwalks are wet and slippery, especially near waterfalls. No flip-flops on trails
Rain jacket and layers even in summer, as the lakes create their own microclimate and temperatures drop in the canyon
Swimwear for Korana River. Sunscreen, hat, and at least 1.5 litres of water per person for full-day park visits

culturalTips.title: Language Basics
culturalTips.text: Learn "Dobar dan" (good day), "Hvala" (thank you), and "Molim" (please). Croatian staff appreciate any effort. English is widely spoken at tourist sites but less common in rural Lika villages.

culturalTips.title: Lika Cuisine
culturalTips.text: The Lika region is known for lamb (janjetina), trout, cheese (škripavac), and dishes cooked under the peka (iron bell). Portions are enormous and meant for sharing. Finish with rakija, homemade fruit brandy offered as a welcome gesture.

culturalTips.title: Nature Respect
culturalTips.text: Swimming in the Plitvice lakes is strictly forbidden, as the travertine ecosystem is extremely fragile. Stay on boardwalks, don't touch the water, and never feed wildlife. Fines for violations are steep and enforced.

culturalTips.title: Coffee Culture
culturalTips.text: Croatians take coffee seriously, and "ići na kavu" (going for coffee) is a social ritual that can last hours. If invited for coffee, accept. Turkish coffee (kava) and espresso are standard. It's rude to rush.

culturalTips.title: Guesthouse Etiquette
culturalTips.text: Many Plitvice visitors stay in family-run guesthouses (sobe). Hosts often offer homemade food, rakija, and local tips. Accepting hospitality is important, as declining food can seem rude. A small gift from home is appreciated.

culturalTips.title: Wildlife Awareness
culturalTips.text: Brown bears, wolves, and lynx live in the forests around Plitvice, Europe's richest large-mammal habitat. They're shy and avoid humans but never leave food out. Dawn and dusk are when you're most likely to spot deer and foxes.
